advances: An exact actual-body obstruction to the following integer-completion pruning prescription: replace expensive supports of arity r+1 by supports of arity at most r using the integer points in their convex hulls, and pay for the removed score by a fixed multiple of the capacities at newly completed integer sites. In the construction below, all of those newly completed sites coincide with the target. The unrestricted fractional packing and its full dual are computed at every target and cutoff. Lowering the allowed arity by just one loses an unbounded factor, although every expensive support has the same positive coefficients and the same root cost. This is a local pruning obstruction, not a counterexample to the bound for the unrestricted score at scale W/2^n.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The exact root-cost, full-occurrence primal and dual, and arbitrary-support equivalence are used through `793210f8a4be3647`; the distinct integral-hitting notation is used through `488f0a583886b5fc`. Every geometric, combinatorial, optimization, and limiting assertion for the new actual bodies is proved above.
proof:
First, g_r is continuous, convex, and positively homogeneous. It is nonnegative and vanishes only at zero. Indeed, if every coordinate is nonnegative it is their sum. Otherwise put \(t=\max_i(-x_i)>0\). Since \(\sum_i x_i\ge-rt\), one has \(g_r(x)\ge t>0\).

The set \(\{x\in\mathbb R^r:g_r(x)\le1\}\) is exactly the simplex
\(\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_r,-\mathbf1_r\}\).
To verify this directly, for a point x define
\[
 \lambda_0=\frac{1-\sum_i x_i}{r+1},\qquad
 \lambda_i=x_i+\lambda_0\quad(1\le i\le r).
\]
These numbers always sum to one and give
\(x=\sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf e_i-\lambda_0\mathbf1_r\).
They are all nonnegative exactly when
\(\lambda_0\ge\max\{0,-x_1,\ldots,-x_r\}\), which is exactly \(g_r(x)\le1\).

It follows that \(Q=\{x:G(x)\le1\}\) is the convex hull of all the E_b. For one inclusion, G is convex, G=1 at each displayed vertex, and zero is a convex combination of any E_b. For the other, write each nonzero block as \(x^{(b)}=g_r(x^{(b)})q_b\), where \(g_r(q_b)=1\). Each q_b, embedded in its block, lies in the simplex just identified. The numbers \(g_r(x^{(b)})\) sum to at most one. Combining these convex representations and placing the remaining coefficient at zero expresses x as a convex combination of the displayed vertices. In particular Q is a compact full-dimensional rational polytope: it is bounded by its finite vertex description and contains a neighborhood of zero because G is continuous and G(0)=0. The function \(1-(1-\epsilon)G\) is concave and lies in [epsilon,1] on Q. Formula (1) consequently defines a compact convex body with nonempty interior. It is a rational polytope because G is a finite sum of maxima of rational linear functions, hence itself the maximum of finitely many rational linear functions; the inequalities in (1) become finitely many rational affine inequalities.

For an integer block z, g_r(z) is a nonnegative integer, and it is at least one whenever z is nonzero. Hence an integer x with G(x)<=1 has at most one nonzero block. In the single-block simplex, the coefficients just displayed have \(0\le\lambda_0\le1\). If \(0<\lambda_0<1\), then every integer coordinate z_i is nonnegative because \(z_i\ge-\lambda_0>-1\), while \(\sum_i z_i<1\). Thus z=0. If \(\lambda_0=0\), the nonnegative integer coordinates sum to one, giving a basis vertex. If \(\lambda_0=1\), every coordinate is at least -1 and their sum is -r, forcing z=-\(\mathbf1_r\). This proves that the complete lattice support of Q consists exactly of zero and its listed vertices, and proves (7) as well. G equals zero at zero and one at every listed vertex, so the fibers in (1) have lengths one and epsilon respectively. This proves (2), including emptiness of every unlisted integer fiber. The actual concavity of the volume roots is the concavity of the height in (1); no abstract log-concave table is being substituted for the actual body.

Next classify every barycentric representation of zero from D, including representations of arbitrary arity. In block b, the coefficient of \(\mathbf e_{b,i}\) must equal the coefficient of \(\mathbf v_{b,0}\), since these are respectively the positive and negative contributions to that coordinate. Thus, whenever any vertex of block b occurs with positive coefficient, all r+1 vertices of that block occur, and they have equal coefficients. This also applies when the central source occurs. Therefore any support omitting zero is a union of whole blocks E_b. Each one E_b is affinely independent: if
\(\sum_{i=1}^r c_i(\mathbf e_{b,i}+\mathbf1_b)=0\), where \(\mathbf1_b=\sum_i\mathbf e_{b,i}\), then its coordinate equations give \(c_i+\sum_jc_j=0\); summing gives \((r+1)\sum_jc_j=0\), and all c_i vanish. Zero has its unique positive coefficients \(1/(r+1)\) in that simplex.

A union of t>=2 whole blocks has t(r+1) vertices but affine span of dimension tr. The span dimension is tr because zero lies in each block's affine hull and the block coordinate spaces are independent. Such a union is affinely dependent since \(t(r+1)>tr+1\). A support consisting of zero and at least one whole block is also affinely dependent, because zero is already a convex combination of that block. Consequently the FULL canonical independent family at zero is exactly
\[
 \mathcal E_{\mathbf0}=\{\{\mathbf0\},E_1,\ldots,E_m\}.
\tag{9}
\]
The singleton has cost zero. All the sources on E_b have actual root volume epsilon (d=1), so their root-volume mean is epsilon and their cost is \(\log(1/\epsilon)=L_\star\). This verifies the costs in the exact finite formulation of `793210f8a4be3647`.

If L<L_star, the only allowed independent support in (9) is the singleton. Its capacity is one, so its primal optimum is one and the dual vector \(u_{\mathbf0}=1\), \(u_{\mathbf I}=0\) otherwise has objective one. If L>=L_star, put mass one on the central singleton and mass epsilon on each E_b. Every noncentral source belongs to exactly one E_b and receives its FULL epsilon charge. The center receives exactly its singleton charge one. Thus the simultaneous primal mass is \(1+m\epsilon\). The dual vector
\[
 u_{\mathbf0}=1,\qquad
 u_{\mathbf v_{b,i}}=\frac1{r+1}\quad(1\le b\le m,\ 0\le i\le r)
\tag{10}
\]
is feasible, since its sum on every E_b is exactly one, and its objective is exactly \(1+m\epsilon\). Weak duality proves optimality. This is a calculation in the FULL incidence dual, not a coefficient-weighted dual: the primal incidence columns are \(\mathbf1_{E_b}\) and the dual constraints are \(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E_b}u_{\mathbf I}\ge1\).

One can also check the arbitrary-support formulation directly. Any component omitting zero contains at least one whole E_b, its root mean is epsilon, and its cost is L_star. Any component containing zero charges its entire mass to the center, so all such masses together are at most one. Assign each component omitting zero to one block it contains. In a fixed assigned block every vertex is charged the full mass of each assigned component, so the sum of those masses is at most epsilon. Summing over m blocks gives at most m epsilon. Thus no arbitrary arity, non-independent support, or choice of unequal coefficients increases the values just proved. For L<L_star every allowed component must contain zero. For L>=L_star the same assignment bounds all costs and supports without a cutoff restriction.

For integral hitting, the singleton requires deleting zero, at weight one. At the larger cutoff each disjoint E_b also requires at least one deleted vertex, of weight epsilon. Choosing one vertex from each block attains \(1+m\epsilon\); at smaller cutoffs zero alone attains one. This proves (3) separately for the two optimization problems.

Every listed vertex is extreme in Q. For a positive basis vertex \(\mathbf e_{b,i}\), the functional x->\(x_i^{(b)}\) uniquely maximizes at that vertex among D. For the negative vertex \(\mathbf v_{b,0}\), the functional x->\(-\sum_i x_i^{(b)}\) uniquely maximizes there, with value r. Any positive barycentric representation of a uniquely maximizing point uses only that point, since the average of any strictly smaller functional value with positive coefficient is strictly smaller. This proves (4), including the arbitrary-support version, and shows that no unlisted target in D was omitted. Optimizing (3)-(4) over all cutoffs gives (5): the first branch uses cutoff zero and the second uses cutoff L_star, because its mass is constant thereafter and its denominator increases.

Now impose the arity cap r solely for the pruning comparison. The block classification shows that a component at target zero omitting zero has at least r+1 sources, so no such component is allowed. Every retained component consequently charges its full mass to zero, and their aggregate mass is at most one. The central singleton attains one at every cutoff. The uniquely maximizing functionals at all other targets still force singleton supports and give epsilon. This proves (6) even with arbitrary original coefficients and non-independent supports.

The uniform coefficients on each E_b have entropy
\(-\sum_{i=0}^r(r+1)^{-1}\log((r+1)^{-1})=\log(r+1)\).
All capacities of the m-component scheme are globally feasible because its supports are disjoint. By (7), every new integer site generated by completing any of these simplices is the same central site, already present in D; its total physical capacity remains one. Even if an exchange may use the original vertices as well as the completion, every replacement at zero of arity at most r must contain zero, by the same block classification. Thus its total feasible replacement mass is at most one, independently of how the components are split or how their positive coefficients are chosen. Treating that one site as a separate reserve for each original simplex would count the same original capacity repeatedly and would violate the full shared-capacity convention.

Finally m=\(2^{2r}\) gives m epsilon=\(2^r\), proving both expressions in (8). They tend to infinity because \(2^r/r\) tends to infinity. Multiplying the second expression by the entropy \(\log(r+1)\) cannot restore a bounded ratio. These calculations pinpoint the first false step in the proposed compensation: convexity produces a valid positive integer completion for each individual support but supplies no disjoint or bounded-congestion capacity across different supports. All targets, all root costs, all supports, and all cutoffs of the unrestricted score were retained in (3)-(5). The construction does not give a vanishing ratio \(2^n\mathcal B_1(w)/W\), and no conclusion refuting the unrestricted bridge or the locked weak Oertel conjecture is drawn.
For (11), its right side is 2A by (6)-(7), whereas its left side tends to infinity by (8), so choosing a sufficiently large r gives the stated violation.
statement:
Use D, W, w, the affinely independent support family \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\), the full-occurrence fractional packing \(P_d(\mathbf J,L)\), and the score \(\mathcal B_d(w)\) exactly as in accepted fact `793210f8a4be3647`. Use the integral hitting mass \(m_d(\mathbf J,L;w)\) separately, with precisely the meaning given in accepted fact `488f0a583886b5fc`: it is the minimum weight of a set meeting every allowed support, not the fractional LP dual. The semicolon in that notation only displays the table argument. All logarithms are natural.

For integers r>=2 and m>=1, set n=mr, d=1, and \(\epsilon=2^{-r}\). Index the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^n\) by \(\mathbf e_{b,i}\), where 1<=b<=m and 1<=i<=r. Set
\[
 \mathbf v_{b,0}=-\sum_{i=1}^r\mathbf e_{b,i},\qquad
 \mathbf v_{b,i}=\mathbf e_{b,i}\quad(1\le i\le r),\qquad
 E_b=\{\mathbf v_{b,0},\ldots,\mathbf v_{b,r}\}.
\]
For \(x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})\in\mathbb R^{mr}\), with \(x^{(b)}\in\mathbb R^r\), define
\[
 g_r(x^{(b)})=\sum_{i=1}^r x_i^{(b)}
 +(r+1)\max\{0,-x_1^{(b)},\ldots,-x_r^{(b)}\},\qquad
 G(x)=\sum_{b=1}^m g_r(x^{(b)}),
\]
and take the rational convex body
\[
 C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:
             G(x)\le1,\quad 0\le y\le1-(1-\epsilon)G(x)\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Here G is an explicitly defined base gauge, not the logarithmic gap \(G_E\) in `488f0a583886b5fc`; no potential lifting or change of the integer lattice is used. Retain the locked \(S=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R)\) and \(h_S\). Its complete positive fiber table is
\[
 D=\{\mathbf0\}\cup\bigcup_{b=1}^m E_b,\qquad
 w_{\mathbf0}=1,\qquad w_{\mathbf v_{b,i}}=\epsilon,\qquad
 W=1+m(r+1)\epsilon.
\tag{2}
\]
Every other integer fiber is empty. Write \(L_\star=\log(1/\epsilon)=r\log2\), reserving L for an arbitrary cutoff. At every cutoff L>=0, the FULL unrestricted programs are
\[
 P_1(\mathbf0,L)=m_1(\mathbf0,L;w)=
 \begin{cases}
   1,&0\le L<L_\star,\\
   1+m\epsilon,&L\ge L_\star,
 \end{cases}
\tag{3}
\]
and, for every \(\mathbf v\in D\setminus\{\mathbf0\}\),
\[
 P_1(\mathbf v,L)=m_1(\mathbf v,L;w)=\epsilon.
\tag{4}
\]
Equality of the two values here is a proved feature of this example, not an identification of fractional duality with integral hitting. In particular
\[
 \mathcal B_1(w)=
 \max\left\{1,\frac{1+m\epsilon}{1+L_\star}\right\}.
\tag{5}
\]

Define \(P_1^{(\le r)}(\mathbf J,L)\) by allowing only components with at most r distinct sources in the original arbitrary-support formulation of `793210f8a4be3647`, keeping every original full-occurrence capacity, every positive coefficient, the same costs, and the same target and cutoff. Define its optimized score by the same maximum over ALL targets and ALL cutoffs. Then
\[
 P_1^{(\le r)}(\mathbf0,L)=1,\qquad
 P_1^{(\le r)}(\mathbf v,L)=\epsilon,\qquad
 \mathcal B_1^{(\le r)}(w)=1
 \quad(L\ge0,\ \mathbf v\in D\setminus\{\mathbf0\}).
\tag{6}
\]
Moreover
\[
 \left(\bigcup_{b=1}^m\operatorname{conv}E_b\cap\mathbb Z^n\right)
       \setminus\bigcup_{b=1}^m E_b=\{\mathbf0\},
 \qquad \sum_{\mathbf I\in\{\mathbf0\}}w_{\mathbf I}=1.
\tag{7}
\]
The component on E_b with mass \(x_b=\epsilon\) and coefficients \(1/(r+1)\) at all its sources is feasible simultaneously for every b. Its cost is exactly \(L_\star\), its barycentric entropy is \(\log(r+1)\), and its FULL charge at each source is \(\epsilon\). These m components have total mass \(m\epsilon\); their total score contribution at cutoff \(L_\star\) is \(m\epsilon/(1+L_\star)\).

Thus, with m=\(2^{2r}\) and r tending to infinity,
\[
 \frac{\mathcal B_1(w)}{\mathcal B_1^{(\le r)}(w)}
 \ \ge\ \frac{1+2^r}{1+r\log2}\longrightarrow\infty,
 \qquad
 \frac{\sum_b x_b/(1+L_\star)}
      {\sum_{\mathbf I\in\{\mathbf0\}}w_{\mathbf I}}
 =\frac{2^r}{1+r\log2}\longrightarrow\infty.
\tag{8}
\]
Even after allowing arbitrary low-arity replacements using all original vertices and all their integer completions, the shared capacity available for those replacements at target zero is only one. Consequently there is no absolute-factor pruning guarantee of the prescription in ADVANCES. More strongly, no universal inequality can charge either the discarded normalized mass, or that mass multiplied by the uniform barycentric entropy \(\log(r+1)\), solely to the additional capacities in (7).
In particular, for every finite A>=0, some body (1) violates the concrete proposed pruning estimate
\[
 \mathcal B_1(w)\le
 A\left(\mathcal B_1^{(\le r)}(w)
       +\sum_{\mathbf I\in\{\mathbf0\}}w_{\mathbf I}\right).
\tag{11}
\]
The estimate uses the same physical capacities before and after the exchange; it does not give separate copies of the central capacity to different supports.
